Final answer is in `final.py`. Search score 0.571, 16 of 24 scorer calls used, done in the default 15-minute mode (04:04 to 04:15).

| candidate | harness dev | fresh seeds 201-206 | scorer search |
|---|---|---|---|
| baseline LRU | 0.419 | 0.454 | 0.365 |
| first champion: LIRS, 1% HIR | 0.524 | 0.519 | 0.563 |
| final: adaptive LIRS | 0.528 | 0.524 | 0.571 |

**What final.py is.** A LIRS cache (low inter-reference recency set) whose small HIR queue adapts in size. A shadow LRU of the last capacity-many distinct keys tells when plain LRU would have hit a miss, and the HIR queue grows by one. It shrinks by 25 when a key demoted from the LIR set and then evicted is requested again, and by one for every eight HIR slots evicted unused. The per-trace scorer detail shows why it beats LRU: loops longer than capacity keep a fixed resident set instead of thrashing, and the adaptation recovers the recency hits that plain LIRS gives up. Runtime is about 2 seconds per 720k requests locally, well under the 8-second limit.

**Families tried in step 3**, all on the harness and the scorer where listed: ARC 0.407, S3-FIFO 0.465, 2Q 0.466, LIRS 0.563. W-TinyLFU and LFU with dynamic aging lost on the harness and were not scored. LIRS won by a wide margin on the loop-style traces.

**One caveat worth knowing.** My harness and the scorer disagreed on the adaptive variants: the scorer's recency trace rewards them much more than my generated one does. An earlier adaptive version (scorer 0.570) collapsed on shifting loops on held-out harness seeds because its shrink signal never fired in pure loops. The final version fixes that and beats plain LIRS on both harness seed sets and the scorer, so I trust it to generalize, but the harness-only margin over plain LIRS is small.

The candidate log with every variant, its scores, and why it was kept or dropped is in `log.md` beside the candidates.
